Does socialism contain an opposition analogous to the philosophical opposition between those who affirm and those who deny that human beings can attain wisdom?
If Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism coincides with Hegel’s philosophy, then clearly it must agree with Hegel that wisdom is attainable.
And it is easy to see that this is indeed the case.

Once we accept the thesis—which will become fully convincing only at the end of this book—that human existence in communist society, and only there, is perfectly conscious of itself, then the problem of attaining wisdom becomes identical with the problem of attaining communism.

Indeed, one of Comrade Stalin’s principal achievements—and perhaps his principal theoretical achievement—is his claim that socialism can be built in a single country. The success of this active construction, carried out under Comrade Stalin, provides striking confirmation of that claim.
Socialism has therefore moved out of a distant and more or less uncertain future into the clear light of actual present reality.

And, as Comrade Stalin has repeatedly shown, the reality of socialism in one country guarantees that sooner or later it can spread across the whole earth, thereby creating the conditions necessary for the realization of communism.
The essence of Stalinism therefore consists not only in affirming that communism—and hence “wisdom”—is attainable, but also in identifying the active path by which it can actually be attained.
On this point, Comrade Stalin, building on the doctrine of his teacher and friend, the great Lenin, unquestionably went further than Marx.
But he did not break with Marx. On the contrary, he merely developed Marx’s fundamental propositions.

For Marx’s “scientific” socialism differs from the “utopian” socialism of his non-Hegelian predecessors precisely because it does not merely describe communism. It shows the path toward communism from the actually existing social and political world.
The claim that communism, and therefore wisdom, can be attained is thus fundamental to Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism as a whole.

Yet just as philosophy contains both the true affirmation that wisdom is attainable and the mistaken denial that it is, socialism too contains, alongside authentic Marxism, a current that denies that communism can ever actually be reached.
We need only look at social democracy, which has flourished so much in the West in recent years.

Without even discussing what the social democrats make of communism—which they speak of much as Christian mystics speak of the “Second Coming of Christ”—we can simply note how ingeniously they have managed to turn socialism into a mystical affair belonging to the future.

By rejecting the active means established by Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, they made the goal itself unreal. And in fact, from the social-democratic point of view, the pursuit of socialism is just as “endless” as the endless pursuit of “wisdom” undertaken by philosophers who deny that wisdom can actually be reached under real conditions. So just as those philosophers either fell into skeptical nihilism or sought refuge in “God,” the reformists of social democracy either took on an openly religious character, as in the Anglo-Saxon countries, or drifted toward skeptical and nihilistic anarchism.

There is little point, however, in spending too much time over this political corpse. The social democrats will soon disappear from the historical stage and, one hopes, never return. We might even say that they are already dead. The ancient Romans held that one should speak well of the dead or say nothing at all. Since we have nothing good to say about the social democrats, it is probably best to stop talking about them altogether.

I have mentioned them here only to point out that socialism contains the same two opposing tendencies that we find in philosophy. And as long as the unpleasant memory of Marx’s Doctrine survives in the distorted form given to it by social democracy, we should avoid the worn-out word “Marxism” and use the admittedly cumbersome but much more precise expression “Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.”

To sum up, then, Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism fully coincides with philosophy in its Hegelian form. Its ultimate and attainable ideal of human existence is complete self-awareness: the ability of a human being to answer convincingly every meaningful question about his life and activity.

From the standpoint of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, however—and this is where it differs from Hegel—that ideal has not yet been reached. “Wisdom” will become possible only in communist society. Before communism, even in a socialist society, we can only strive toward wisdom. And this striving is always at once collective, theoretical and intellectual, and practical and active.
In other words, before communism there can only be philosophy in the strict sense of the word—but a philosophy that knows it will reach its goal.
We began with the ancient Greek saying of the “sage,” the saying on which all later philosophy rests, and from it we eventually arrived at a final definition of the essence of Hegelian philosophy.
We then began from Soviet revolutionary and socialist reality and traced it back to its Marxist intellectual origins. Once again, we were forced to arrive at Hegelianism.

We can therefore say that Hegel’s conception appears, on the one hand, as the logical culmination of the intellectual and historical development of philosophy and, on the other, as the starting point of the active and historical process through which communism is gradually and consciously realized.
As we already know, that conception comes down to this.

“Wisdom” (Sophia) is nothing other than complete self-awareness, or complete consciousness of oneself. It is expressed in the fact that a human being can himself answer convincingly every meaningful question that can be put to him—or that he can put to himself—about his life and his actions in the material world of space and time.
Philo-sophy, for its part, is the effort to attain wisdom. More specifically, it is the art of asking these kinds of questions and the attempt to answer at least some of them.
Philosophy can reach its goal—that is, transform itself into wisdom—if and only if a particular set of sociopolitical or historical conditions is realized in the world.

For this reason, striving for wisdom in the broad sense necessarily includes more than philosophy in the narrow sense, more than the intellectual development of humanity’s theoretical knowledge. It also includes the active development of the historical conditions under which human beings live.
History as a whole therefore consists of two parallel processes:
the real, active, sociopolitical process that leads to the establishment, throughout the entire world, of the final and “ideal” sociopolitical order;

the intellectual and cognitive process that corresponds to the first, depends on it, and includes philo-sophy as the expression of the self-consciousness of the humanity that is actually carrying out that first process.

The completion of history therefore means the simultaneous completion of both processes. Reaching the sociopolitical ideal means, at the same time, reaching philosophy’s ideal of knowledge—that is, reaching the ideal of “wisdom.”

It follows that no one can consciously strive for “wisdom,” and therefore truly be a philosopher, without also striving toward the sociopolitical ideal. And conversely, it is hardly possible to strive with full awareness toward that sociopolitical ideal without at the same time striving for “wisdom”—that is, without being, to some degree, a “philosopher.”
Hegel on the one hand, and Marx, Lenin, and Stalin on the other, are in complete agreement about all of this.

Their only difference is that Hegel wrongly believed that the sociopolitical ideal had already been reached in his time. This is why he could regard himself not merely as a philosopher but already as a sage. Marx, and after him Lenin and Stalin, knew that this ideal had not yet been reached, even in our own time.
But what interests us here is not what Hegel thought about himself or his own age. What matters is what he thought about philosophy.

And on that point he was entirely correct: philosophy, understood as the striving for a wisdom that is attainable but has not yet been attained, necessarily presupposes a genuinely active process through which the “ideal” society and State are gradually constructed.

At first sight, Hegel’s inclusion of real activity as an essential part of philosophy and wisdom—and the same inclusion in Marxism, Leninism, and Stalinism—may seem to contradict the whole philosophical tradition that came before him.
In fact, it does nothing of the kind. That is what we now need to examine.

If we set aside the degenerate philosophers—few at first, but multiplying horribly in the West in recent times—we can say that every philosopher worthy of the name has agreed that the ideal of “wisdom” toward which philosophy strives is not merely a theoretical and intellectual ideal. It is also an ethical, or moral, ideal.
The “sage” possesses not only perfect knowledge. He is also—and perhaps above all—a human being who has reached ethical perfection.

And since the philosopher strives toward wisdom, since he tries as far as he can to approach the ideal of the sage, he must concern himself not only with his theoretical and intellectual development but also with his ethical improvement.

So anyone who speaks about ethics or “morality” must consider not only the theoretical, cognitive, inactive, or “passive” and contemplative side of existence, but also its practical, “active,” and creative side.
Hegel’s inclusion of the active element in the concept of philosophy, later taken up by Marx, Lenin, and Stalin, is therefore not a break with philosophical tradition.

On the contrary, here as elsewhere, Hegel merely develops and clarifies that tradition. Marx, Lenin, and Stalin follow him in this. He makes the tradition fully conscious of itself by bringing out all the assumptions and consequences that had always been contained within it.

To understand more clearly the character and meaning of this clarification of the traditional idea of the philosopher and the sage, carried out by Hegel, Marx, Lenin, and Stalin, we must first notice that the ethical aspect of “wisdom” we are discussing now does not contradict the theoretical aspect discussed so far.
The two are in fact inseparably connected.
They are not two independent qualities accidentally joined together, qualities that could therefore be separated again. They are two sides, or two aspects, of one and the same thing.
If we look at wisdom from the standpoint of knowledge, we must define it as perfect knowledge. If we look at it from the standpoint of action, we must define it as perfect ethical life.
Here is how this should be understood.

When we consider “wisdom” as knowledge, we define it as the ability to answer, meaningfully and convincingly, whether in writing or aloud, every question that can be asked about the life and actions of the person who possesses it.

To answer “meaningfully” means to answer in such a way that another person can understand the answer. To answer “convincingly” means to answer in such a way that the answer satisfies that other person.
But the words “understand” and “satisfy” have two meanings—and, as we will see, this ambiguity is far from accidental. They can be used in both a theoretical and an ethical sense.

We can say, for example, “I don’t understand English,” or “your knowledge is unsatisfactory.” But we can also say, “I don’t understand how you can think that way,” or “your behavior is unsatisfactory.”
So even when someone answers a question in a theoretically meaningful and satisfactory way, he may still encounter ethical “incomprehension” and ethical “dissatisfaction.”

In other words, we may refuse to answer a question not only because we do not know what to say, but because answering would make us feel ashamed, would trouble our conscience, or would simply be terrifying.
Nothing like this, however, can ever happen to the “sage”—or at least that is what philosophical tradition claims.
The sage can always answer any question put to him. Doing so will never confront him with a crisis of conscience, nor will it terrify him.
This means that ethical perfection is being attributed to him, because he can always answer for everything he has done.

Since he regards his actions as ethically right, he will never be ashamed to speak about them. And even if speaking openly could bring disastrous consequences upon him, those consequences will never prevent him from speaking.
It is therefore clear that this ideal of the philosophical tradition is also the ideal of the revolutionary and socialist tradition.

How, then, did certain sorry philosophers manage to forget all of this and maintain that philosophy is an “abstract science” with nothing to do with life, concerned exclusively with knowledge and having nothing in common with action?
How could they say that “no one cares about the philosopher’s private life”?
To understand how this happened, we need to return to what we have already said about the individualist and collectivist conceptions of wisdom and of the path toward it—that is, of philosophy.

We can say that, before Hegel, all philosophical traditions assumed that the individual could strive toward the ideal of wisdom on his own and, as some thinkers believed, could even reach it independently of the conditions around him.

Of course, philosophers knew perfectly well that external circumstances—illness, persecution by the State, and so on—could interfere with a thinker’s work. The death of Socrates, after all, will remain forever engraved in the memory of philosophers.
But these things were not thought to have any special philosophical importance. They were regarded as purely external conditions, with no connection to philosophy itself.
Since a philosopher had to eat, drink, and sleep, he naturally also had to look after the other conditions required for staying alive, including his personal safety.
In short, the philosopher merely had to make sure that external conditions did not disturb him. His philosophical work itself was supposed to remain independent of them.
Plato, it is true, repeatedly emphasizes that Socrates took an active part in the political and military life of Athens, tried to reform it, and eventually paid for that attempt with his life.
Plato himself also believed that governing the ideal State was the philosopher’s first and most fundamental duty.
Yet he also assumed that the philosopher acquires knowledge independently of his political life and only afterward puts that knowledge into practice.

The philosopher could therefore remain inactive if he wished. If he forced himself to enter public affairs, he did so not for his own sake or for the sake of philosophy, but for moral reasons—solely for the good of other people.
At any rate, Plato honestly includes both the cognitive and the practical sides within his concept of philosophy and connects them to one another.
Very soon, however, Aristotle, seeing how little success his teacher’s political efforts had achieved, brought the theoretical and contemplative element to the foreground.

In his vigorous younger years he could still count the education of Alexander of Macedon among his achievements. But as he grew older, and especially after the death of his famous pupil, he withdrew more and more from active life and shut himself away within theoretical contemplation.
After Aristotle, the separation between philosophy and life continued to deepen.
This separation became especially striking under the Roman Empire, among the Stoics, Epicureans, and Skeptics.

It was then—particularly among the Stoics—that the familiar image of a distinctively “philosophical” attitude toward life took shape: the image of “sages” who regarded with equal indifference everything that did not affect them personally, or more precisely everything that did not affect their intellectual activity.

Part of the blame undoubtedly lay with external circumstances. Under the Roman Empire, any political or social attempt at reform seemed hopeless. Those who thought the world around them was far from ideal simply “withdrew from the world.”
Powerless and inactive criticism did continue.
The ideal of the “fearless” sage was still alive, after all, and more than one philosopher in those days paid with his life for answering openly the questions put to him.
But little by little, silence—the child of fear—came to seem compatible with the dignity of a philosopher.
The Platonic ideal of the philosopher as politician and reformer therefore gave way to the ideal of the “sage” sealed inside his own fortress, far removed from the world and from public life.
The whole idea of the philosopher’s and the sage’s moral conduct was therefore fundamentally transformed.

The philosopher was no longer expected to educate other people and reform the world so that others would accept the answers he gave about his own life, or so that the world would appear “understandable” and “satisfactory” to everyone.
He knew that his morally perfect life would meet with incomprehension from a corrupt world.
But he could reassure himself: what other people thought was no longer his concern.
